posts.headline: Leg pain ==isn't always sciatica==

slides.heading: True sciatica
slides.body: The sciatic nerve being irritated — pain travelling from the lower back into the buttock and down the leg.

slides.heading: Or referred pain
slides.body: A lot of “sciatica” is referred pain from the glutes and deep hip muscles, mimicking the same route.

slides.heading: The distinction matters
slides.body: The two respond to different work. It feels identical to you. It isn’t identical to treat.

slides.heading: Worth mentioning
slides.body: Pins and needles, numbness, whether it’s worse sitting or standing, whether it goes past the knee.

posts.sub: Glute and deep hip muscles refer pain down almost exactly the same route.

posts.headline: Leg pain worse ==when you sit down?==
posts.sub: Whether it's worse sitting or standing changes where we look.

posts.headline: Lower back pain ==often starts at the hips==

slides.heading: Hips
slides.body: Tight hip flexors from sitting pull on the pelvis, and the lower back picks up the slack.

slides.heading: Glutes
slides.body: If they aren’t doing their job, the lower back does it instead.

slides.heading: Hamstrings
slides.body: Tight hamstrings tilt the pelvis and change how the spine loads.

slides.heading: So we don’t just rub the sore bit
slides.body: We assess hips, glutes and hamstrings as part of any lower back session.

posts.sub: Tight hip flexors and quiet glutes leave the lower back doing the work.

posts.headline: Back or neck pain for months? ==Get it assessed==
posts.sub: The Back & Neck Pain MOT: proper assessment first, then treatment.

posts.headline: Tension headaches ==often start in your neck==

slides.heading: Where they begin
slides.body: Tension headaches often start as tightness at the base of the skull and up into the jaw.

slides.heading: The common pattern
slides.body: Long screen hours, shoulders creeping up, head drifting forward toward the monitor.

slides.heading: Worth treating the neck
slides.body: Not just taking something for the head.

posts.sub: Tightness at the base of the skull after long screen hours.

posts.headline: What sitting at a desk ==does to your body==

slides.heading: Hip flexors shorten
slides.body: Hours in the same seated position, every working day.

slides.heading: Glutes switch off
slides.body: They stop contributing, and something else covers for them.

slides.heading: Upper back rounds
slides.body: Shoulders drift forward toward the keyboard.

slides.heading: Neck takes the strain
slides.body: Holding your head where the screen is, not where it wants to be.

slides.heading: None of it is dramatic
slides.body: All of it adds up. Then you pick up a bag and it goes.

posts.sub: Hip flexors shorten, glutes switch off, the neck takes the strain.

posts.headline: What a muscle knot ==actually is==

slides.heading: A tight, sensitive band
slides.body: Within a muscle. Press it and it often refers pain somewhere else entirely.

slides.heading: That’s why
slides.body: A knot in your shoulder can be felt down your arm, and one in your glute down your leg.

slides.heading: Trigger point work is slow
slides.body: Specific and deliberate. It isn’t the same as hard pressure everywhere.

posts.sub: A tight band that refers pain elsewhere — which is why we treat elsewhere.

posts.headline: Struggling to reach ==behind your back?==
posts.sub: Frozen shoulder goes through stages, and each one needs different work.

posts.headline: Heel pain on your ==first steps of the day?==

slides.heading: The classic pattern
slides.body: Sharp heel pain on the first few steps out of bed, easing as you move about.

slides.heading: The foot is where you feel it
slides.body: The calf is very often where the problem actually is.

slides.heading: So we treat all three
slides.body: Calf, achilles and foot together, rather than just working the sore heel.

posts.sub: Classic plantar fasciitis. The foot hurts, but the calf is often the cause.

posts.headline: Stretching your hamstrings ==isn't working?==

posts.headline: Hip pain is often ==felt somewhere else==

posts.headline: Tennis elbow from ==a keyboard, not a racket==

posts.headline: Shin splints usually mean ==too much, too soon==
posts.sub: Deal with it at uncomfortable, not at can't-run.

posts.headline: Stiff achilles ==first thing in the morning?==
posts.sub: Eases when you're warm, aches again at night. Don't ignore it.

posts.sub: Relaxation and lymphatic drainage: lighter, slower, completely different.

posts.headline: Why we tell you ==to drink water==

slides.heading: You’ll hear it everywhere
slides.body: The usual explanation — flushing out toxins — isn’t really how it works.

slides.heading: The honest version
slides.body: Hydrated muscle tissue is more pliable and cramps less readily.

slides.heading: So drink the water
slides.body: Just for the actual reason. Turning up dehydrated makes the work harder.

posts.sub: Not to flush toxins. Hydrated muscle is more pliable and cramps less.

posts.headline: The four areas ==runners get tight==

slides.heading: Calves
slides.body: The obvious one. Taking load every step, every mile.

slides.heading: Glutes & hips
slides.body: The ones almost nobody stretches — and behind a lot of “knee” problems.

slides.heading: Hamstrings
slides.body: Usually tight because they’re covering for the glutes, not because they’re short.

slides.heading: Outside of the thigh
slides.body: Where complaints surface, though the cause is usually further up.

posts.sub: Calves, glutes and hips, hamstrings, and the outside of the thigh.

posts.headline: What happens at ==your first sports massage==

slides.heading: 1. We talk
slides.body: What’s wrong, how long it’s been going on, what makes it worse.

slides.heading: 2. We assess
slides.body: How you actually move — that tells us more than pressing on the sore bit.

slides.heading: 3. Treatment
slides.body: Based on what we found. You can talk throughout. “That’s too much” is a complete sentence.

slides.heading: 4. What to do next
slides.body: Something to work on between now and next time.

posts.sub: Talk, assess how you move, treat what we found, then what to do next.
